Neonatal round stingrays (Urolophus halleri) emerge from their mother with a disc width typically measuring 7.2 centimeters [Lb = 7.2 centimeters], though a broader range of 6.3 to 8 centimeters [Lb = 6.3 to 8 centimeters] has been documented in field surveys across Southern California. These dimensions represent the size at which the yolk-dependent embryo transitions to independent foraging, marking the onset of exogenous feeding. This birth size is relatively modest among urolophid species, reflecting a trade-off between maximizing neonatal survivorship and maintaining the mobility of the gravid female. The small disc width at parturition suggests that neonates rely heavily on shallow, protected nursery habitats where predation risk is reduced and benthic invertebrate prey is abundant. The disc width of neonates appears closely linked to maternal body condition and local environmental productivity, with coastal populations in warmer embayments producing slightly larger pups on average. This variability underscores the importance of maternal investment in determining initial offspring size, a factor that can influence early growth trajectories and survival during the critical first months of life. Understanding these baseline measurements provides essential context for comparing developmental patterns across elasmobranch taxa.

Females of Urolophus halleri attain an ultimate disc width averaging 22.4 centimeters [Li = 22.4 centimeters], a figure derived from long-term mark-recapture studies of reproductively active adults in the waters off southern California. Males, by contrast, achieve a substantially larger ultimate disc width of 31 centimeters [Li = 31 centimeters], an unusual pattern of reversed sexual size dimorphism among stingrays. This sex-specific difference in asymptotic body size suggests divergent selective pressures acting on each sex, possibly linked to male-male competition for access to females during the breeding season. Large body size in males may confer advantages during copulation, where clasper-mediated fertilisation requires physical coordination and positioning. The ultimate wet weight for males reaches approximately 1400 grams [Wwi = approximately 1400 grams], representing a robust somatic condition supported by a diet rich in crustaceans and polychaetes. These morphometric data indicate that males invest heavily in somatic growth even after reaching reproductive maturity, a strategy that contrasts with the more size-constrained growth pattern observed in females. The energetic costs of maintaining such a large body size likely influence foraging behavior and habitat use throughout adulthood.

Sexual maturation in round stingrays occurs at distinct disc widths for each sex, providing a clear metric for assessing reproductive maturity in wild populations. Females reach puberty at a disc width of 14.6 centimeters [Lp = 14.6 centimeters], whereas males do so at a slightly smaller 14.4 centimeters [Lp = 14.4 centimeters]. These values correspond to approximately 65 percent of the ultimate disc width for females and 46 percent for males, indicating that males mature at a relatively earlier stage of their overall growth trajectory. The onset of gonadal maturation involves testicular recrudescence in males and ovarian maturation in females, a process that is energetically demanding and closely tied to seasonal temperature cycles. Field data suggest that the age at which these disc widths are attained varies among individuals, influenced by local prey availability and water temperature. The proximity of these two pubertal disc widths suggests that both sexes become reproductively competent at a similar body size, facilitating synchronized breeding events. This reproductive strategy likely maximizes the probability of successful copulation and subsequent fertilization.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 23.6 °C [T = 23.6 °C], the age at birth for Urolophus halleri is approximately 3 months [ab = approximately 3 months], representing the gestation period from internal fertilisation to parturition. This relatively brief developmental period contrasts with the longer gestation durations observed in larger stingray species, where embryonic development may extend beyond six months in some dasyatids. The thermal regime of 23.6 °C [T = 23.6 °C] appears to optimize metabolic rates in the developing embryo, facilitating rapid yolk utilization and organogenesis. Under these same stable thermal conditions (23.6 °C [T = 23.6 °C]), the maximum lifespan recorded for this species reaches 16 years [am = 16 years], a value consistent with estimates from tag-recapture studies in the wild. This longevity is remarkable for a ray of this body size and suggests a slow pace of life, with individuals investing in multiple reproductive events over a prolonged adult phase. The combination of short gestation and long lifespan implies a life history strategy that balances relatively high offspring production in each litter with extended reproductive tenure.

The maximum reproductive rate for round stingrays, observed at 23.6 °C [T = 23.6 °C], reflects the species' capacity for producing litters of 3 to 6 pups [N_R_i = 3 to 6 pups] per reproductive event. Females typically produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = a single litter each year], indicating an annual reproductive cycle synchronized with seasonal warming trends. This annual frequency suggests that the energetic demands of gestation, combined with the need to replenish endogenous reserves, limit the number of litters a female can sustain within a calendar year. Litter size varies considerably among individuals, with larger, older females more frequently producing litters of 5 or 6 pups, while younger breeders tend toward the lower end of the range. The annual reproductive output of this species is thus moderate compared to other small elasmobranchs, aligning with a K-selected life history strategy. The correlation between maternal body size and litter size demonstrates the importance of somatic condition in determining fecundity. These reproductive parameters highlight the species' vulnerability to overfishing, as even modest increases in adult mortality can substantially reduce population recruitment over time.
